sector: Financials / Non-bank Lending (NZ Non-Bank Deposit Taker)
overview: General Capital Limited is a small NZX Main Board-listed financial services holding company whose principal operating subsidiary, General Finance Limited (GFL), is a licensed non-bank deposit taker (NBDT) regulated by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand under the Non-bank Deposit Takers Act 2013 (transitioning to the Deposit Takers Act 2023). GFL raises retail term deposits from ~1,818 depositors and on-lends primarily via short-term, first-mortgage property-secured loans (predominantly bridging/residential finance sourced through a broker network) plus a smaller insurance premium funding book; the group also runs a minor Research & Advisory (corporate finance/listing advisory) segment. For the year ended 31 March 2026, total assets reached NZ$283.7m (+30% YoY), loan receivables NZ$242.5m (+63% YoY), NPAT NZ$2.72m and total equity NZ$31.3m — a genuine but still very small-scale participant at the near-prime end of the NZ non-bank lending market.

business_model.summary: The core economics are a deposit-funded lending spread: GFL borrows via retail term deposits (gross deposit liability NZ$248.1m at FY26, rates 3.35%-8.20%) and lends at commercial mortgage rates (6.45%-10.75% on property loans, up to 20% on insurance premium funding) secured predominantly by first mortgages over NZ residential property (LVR capped at 75%). FY2026 interest income was NZ$24.79m against interest expense of NZ$15.18m, giving net interest income of NZ$9.62m (+8.3% YoY) on average loans of roughly NZ$196.8m — a net interest margin of approximately 4.9%. On top of net interest income the group earns net fee and commission income (NZ$1.36m) and a small research/advisory revenue line (NZ$0.52m), taking total gross profit to NZ$11.57m (+16.4% YoY). Cost-to-income (total operating expenses of NZ$7.57m, including the NZ$576k increase in ECL allowance and a NZ$379k goodwill impairment in the Research & Advisory CGU, against NZ$11.57m gross profit) was approximately 65%, or roughly 60% excluding the ECL charge and one-off impairment — a level typical of a sub-scale NBDT with limited operating leverage; management expects this to improve as the loan book scales. Revenue is largely 'recurring' in the sense that it is a running spread on a rolling book, but it is NOT contractual/subscription revenue — it resets continuously with market interest rates and requires continuous origination and deposit reinvestment to sustain (60% of term deposits are assumed to roll over at maturity per the FY26 liquidity disclosures). The Finance segment generated NZ$3.50m of segment NPAT in FY26 (the Research & Advisory segment posted a small loss after the goodwill impairment).

revenue_streams.name: Net interest income (property-secured first mortgage lending, funded by term deposits)
Net fee and commission income (loan origination, account fees)
Research & Advisory (corporate/listing advisory fees)
revenue_streams.trend: declining/volatile — goodwill impaired NZ$379k in FY26, revenue forecast to fall ~84% in FY27 per management's own impairment-test assumptions

revenue_streams.name: Insurance premium funding (unsecured, but insurer-guaranteed on default)
revenue_streams.percent: included within Finance segment (~2.5% of gross loan book by value)

business_model.customer_type: B2C retail depositors (1,818 term-deposit holders, NZ$248m) funding a book of predominantly B2C/small-business borrowers (1,677 loan exposures) sourced through a mortgage broker network; largely North Island and heavily Auckland-concentrated (76% of loan book value in Auckland, 87.6% North Island)
business_model.geographic_mix: 100% New Zealand. Deposits: Auckland 37%, Wellington 15%, Waikato 10%, Bay of Plenty 7%, Canterbury 9%, other regions and 4% overseas. Loans: Auckland ~76% of book value, North Island ~87.6%, remainder South Island (notably a rapid increase in Otago exposure, NZ$1.1m to NZ$20.3m YoY).

main_competitors: Other NZ non-bank/private mortgage lenders and finance companies (e.g. Basecorp Finance, Prospa/Asset Finance-type lenders, First Mortgage Trust, Pearlfisher/Cressida Capital, Avanti Finance, Bluestone, Liberty Financial)
Registered trading banks (ANZ, BNZ, ASB, Westpac, Kiwibank) at the prime end, and increasingly at the near-prime/bridging end as banks compete for volume in a low-OCR environment
Other rated NBDTs (e.g. Heartland Bank NBDT-heritage products, Xceda Finance, First Credit Union) competing for the same retail term-deposit investor base
Peer-to-peer and private/wholesale mortgage funds competing for both deposit-like capital and borrower demand
competitive_position.market_position: A minor, sub-scale participant. General Finance's NZ$242.5m loan book and NZ$248m deposit book are small relative to the trading banks (each with tens of billions in mortgage books) and even relative to larger non-bank/NBDT peers; General Capital's own market capitalisation (roughly NZ$24-28m at prices of NZ$0.26-0.30/share against ~91.9m shares on issue) underlines the scale gap. The group's edge is a 'near prime' BB-rated niche (Equifax), servicing borrowers and property types (bridging finance, shorter-dated loans) that banks are typically slower or unwilling to fund quickly.

moat_factors.description: The RBNZ NBDT (and future Deposit Takers Act) licence, trust deed and credit-rating requirements are a genuine regulatory barrier to entry for new deposit-taking lenders, but they are not unique to General Finance — several other rated NBDTs and finance companies operate in the same niche, so the barrier protects the category rather than General Finance specifically.

moat_factors.factor: Broker network and speed of decisioning
moat_factors.description: As a specialist non-bank lender, General Finance can approve and settle bridging/short-term property loans faster than trading banks, which is the primary reason borrowers choose non-bank lenders despite a higher interest rate. This is a service/speed advantage rather than a durable structural moat.

moat_factors.factor: Credit rating (Equifax BB, upgraded to Positive outlook Dec-2025)
moat_factors.description: A BB 'near prime' rating from Equifax Australasia is required for NBDTs to offer to retail investors and provides some assurance to depositors, but BB is a sub-investment-grade rating and is materially weaker than the AA-/A+ ratings of the major trading banks holding General Finance's own surplus cash — meaning GFL's own cost of funds will structurally sit above bank deposit rates, and it competes for depositor capital on yield, not safety perception (though the Depositor Compensation Scheme narrows this gap, see Growth Drivers).

moat_factors.factor: Cost of funds disadvantage vs banks
moat_factors.description: General Finance pays materially higher deposit rates (3.35%-8.20%, and a positive credit spread vs banks) to attract retail term deposits than trading banks pay on equivalent products, reflecting its sub-investment-grade profile and smaller scale. This structurally compresses achievable NIM relative to a bank funding the same asset with insured/lower-cost deposits or wholesale funding.

A cost-to-income ratio of ~60-65% on a still-small asset base reflects the fixed overhead (compliance, governance, credit, treasury) NBDTs must carry regardless of size; scale economics favour larger rated peers and, ultimately, the banks.

weaknesses: No pricing power or brand advantage over banks or larger non-bank peers; competes primarily on speed of approval and willingness to lend where banks will not
BB credit rating (sub-investment grade) constrains the depositor base to yield-seeking retail investors rather than institutional or conservative capital
Extremely small absolute scale (NZ$283.7m total assets, NZ$31.3m equity) versus both bank and larger non-bank competitors, limiting diversification and negotiating leverage on funding costs
Heavy geographic and product concentration (76% of loans in Auckland residential property, 97.5% first-mortgage property-secured) leaves the book exposed to a single asset class and city market

Research & Advisory segment is small, lumpy, and now impaired (NZ$379k goodwill write-down in FY26); management's own value-in-use forecast assumes an 84% fall in FY27 segment revenue, underscoring it is not a reliable diversification of earnings

growth_drivers: Loan book scaling: gross loan receivables grew 62.7% in FY26 (NZ$153.98m to NZ$246.42m gross) on the back of 34.3% growth in gross term deposits (NZ$184.72m to NZ$248.05m) — management's own goodwill impairment-test disclosures attribute much of the accelerated deposit inflow to the Depositor Compensation Scheme (effective 1 July 2025) and the strong lending demand to falling OCR. Management guides year-one FY27 loan growth of 27.8% and deposit growth of 34.6%, moderating toward a 20-35% range over the medium term — still a rapid trajectory relative to FY26's already-large base.

Depositor Compensation Scheme (DCS) as a funding tailwind: the DCS went live 1 July 2025, providing up to NZ$100,000 of RBNZ-backed protection per depositor per deposit taker — this narrows the historical 'safety' perception gap between banks and small BB-rated NBDTs like General Finance, and the FY26 annual report explicitly credits the DCS with driving 'higher deposit inflows' that funded loan book growth, together with expanding geographic diversification of the depositor base (Wellington and Christchurch growing faster than Auckland in FY26).

Falling OCR supporting loan demand: the FY26 annual report attributes strong lending demand partly to 'the downward movement of the OCR throughout the year'; further RBNZ easing (OCR at 2.25% as at late 2025) could continue to support borrower demand for bridging/short-term property finance, though it also compresses achievable lending rates over time.

Operating leverage as the book scales: fixed compliance/governance/credit-team costs are largely already in place; continued loan book growth without proportional headcount growth should improve the ~60-65% cost-to-income ratio over time, similar to the pattern seen in FY21-26 (profit before tax growing from NZ$0.12m in FY21 to NZ$3.99m in FY26 while the group scaled ~4x in assets).

Credit rating trajectory: Equifax upgraded General Finance's outlook from 'Stable' to 'Positive' (10 December 2025) while maintaining the BB rating — a ratings upgrade to BB+ or higher would lower GFL's marginal cost of deposit funding and could expand its addressable depositor base.

Bridges Financial Services (insurance premium funding) acquisition (1 November 2024, NZ$7.83m consideration, NZ$1.80m goodwill) demonstrates a bolt-on M&A capability to diversify the lending book into a lower-credit-risk (insurer-guaranteed) asset class; further bolt-on acquisitions in adjacent specialty finance niches are plausible.

Geographic and depositor-base diversification already underway: FY26 saw notable growth in Wellington, Christchurch/Canterbury, and Waikato deposit bases (reducing reliance on Auckland, though loan concentration in Auckland actually increased to 76% from 69.8%).

business.risk: Rapid loan book growth (+62.7% gross in FY26) into a soft/uncertain NZ property market
business.description: A 63% one-year expansion of a property-secured loan book is a classic precursor to future credit losses if underwriting standards loosen to sustain growth, even though current arrears metrics are currently benign. Management's own FY27 forecasts moderate loan growth to 20-35% and explicitly cite 'economic disruption and uncertainty arising from the 2026 Iran conflict' as a reason for caution — indicating management itself views the growth rate as somewhat elevated relative to a normalised trend (3-year average growth was 39.2%, still very high).

business.risk: Expected credit loss (ECL) allowance and provisioning adequacy
business.description: The increase in ECL allowance charged to the P&L was NZ$576,394 in FY26, up from NZ$428,615 in FY25 (roughly a 34% increase, broadly tracking loan book growth). The total impairment allowance stood at NZ$600,771 (0.25% of gross loans) at 31 March 2026, up from NZ$369,227 (also 0.25%) at FY25 — a flat coverage ratio despite very rapid balance growth, meaning provisioning has kept pace proportionally but has not been increased as a precaution against the loan book being materially less 'seasoned' than in prior years (much of the book is <12 months old). Encouragingly, credit quality metrics actually improved in FY26: gross past-due loans fell to NZ$4.40m (1.8% of total loans) from NZ$10.55m (6.9%) in FY25, and Stage 3 (>90 days past due / credit-impaired) balances fell to nil from NZ$2.76m. However, an unseasoned, rapidly-grown book is inherently harder to assess for credit risk than a mature one, and the LVR range on impaired/at-risk loans (67.5%-70.5% in FY26) leaves limited cushion if security property values fall.

97.5% of loans are secured by first mortgage over property, with 90.3% specifically over residential housing; 87.6% of the loan book by value is in the North Island and 76.0% in the Auckland market alone (up from 69.8% in FY25) — a highly correlated single-city, single-asset-class exposure. The six largest loan exposures represent 13.2% of the total portfolio (down from 17.2% in FY25), which is a reasonable improvement but still material concentration for a NZ$246m book. A negative shock to Auckland residential values would disproportionately affect General Finance versus a nationally diversified bank lender.

business.risk: Research & Advisory segment volatility and impairment
business.description: The Research & Advisory CGU carried a NZ$378,730 goodwill impairment in FY26, and management's own value-in-use forecast assumes an 83.8% fall in debt structuring/brokerage revenue and no capital-raising revenue for the next five years — signalling this segment is lumpy, dependent on one-off mandates, and structurally shrinking as a share of group earnings (though it is now immaterial to consolidated NPAT).

Managing Director Brent King has led the group since 2018 (and its predecessor, Dorchester Group, for 17 years) and, together with related entity Snowdon Peak Investments Limited, holds a 10.45% substantial shareholding — meaning his personal financial interests are directly aligned with, but also concentrated in, the company. The board comprises only four directors (one executive, three non-executive, two independent), and a four-person board with a Non-Independent Chairman (due to his own significant shareholding) provides comparatively thin governance depth for an institution taking retail deposits from the public. CFO Vik Singh only joined in May 2025, adding near-term key-person transition risk in a critical control function.

financial.risk: Reliance on retail term deposits and reinvestment/roll-over risk
financial.description: General Finance's entire funding base (NZ$248.05m gross term deposits) is retail term deposits with contractual maturities weighted toward the short end (NZ$129.1m, or 52%, maturing within 6 months per the FY26 contractual cash-flow table). Management's liquidity modelling assumes a 60% term deposit reinvestment rate — i.e. it explicitly plans for 40% of maturing deposits to walk. A loss of depositor confidence (whether company-specific or a broader NBDT-sector event) could trigger a run that the company would need to fund from maturing loans, undrawn bank lines, or asset sales, none of which are guaranteed to be available on short notice.

The FY26 disclosed sensitivity shows a 1% parallel shift in interest rates would move pre-tax profit by roughly NZ$342k (about 8.6% of FY26 NPAT) — a modest but real exposure, driven by differing repricing dates between the loan book and term deposit book. In a falling-OCR environment lending rates may reprice down faster than higher-cost legacy term deposits roll off, compressing NIM over time.

With roughly 91.9m shares on issue and a share price in the NZ$0.26-0.30 range in 2026, GEN's market capitalisation is approximately NZ$24-28m, making it a genuine micro-cap. The top holder (Borneo Capital Limited) owns 34.5-34.6% of the company, and the top 5 substantial holders (Borneo Capital, Brent King/Snowdon Peak, DMX Asset Management, FNZ Custodians and RB New Zealand Pty Ltd) together control 66.4% of shares on issue; the top 20 registered holders control 88.6%. Free float is therefore thin, trading is likely illiquid, and 480 of the company's 687 shareholders (69.9%) each hold fewer than 2,000 shares (a combined 0.1% of the register) — a highly bifurcated, closely-held share register typical of a founder/insider-controlled micro-cap.

financial.risk: Capital ratio headroom versus growth pace
financial.description: The Finance CGU's own goodwill value-in-use model states growth is constrained by the licence/trust deed requirement that the Capital Ratio not fall below 8%. Total equity grew only 7% in FY26 (NZ$29.2m to NZ$31.3m) while total assets grew 30% and gross loans grew 63% — meaning capital is growing far more slowly than the balance sheet. Continued rapid asset growth without commensurate capital raising (retained earnings alone, after a 40%-of-NPAT dividend payout) will progressively erode capital ratio headroom, and further Deposit Takers Act 2023 capital-standard changes (phasing in toward full implementation around 2028) are a live risk to the minimum capital bar NBDTs like General Finance must clear.

regulatory.risk: Transition from the Non-bank Deposit Takers Act 2013 to the Deposit Takers Act 2023
regulatory.description: New Zealand is consolidating bank and non-bank prudential regulation into a single Deposit Takers Act 2023 regime, with the RBNZ expecting the current NBDT Act framework to remain in force until the new regime is fully implemented (around 2028), and further consultation on capital standards, risk weights and loss-absorbing capacity requirements occurring through 2026. For a small, thinly-capitalised NBDT like General Finance, materially higher minimum capital ratios or more conservative risk-weighting under the new regime (designed with larger, systemically important deposit takers in mind) could force either a capital raise, slower growth, or higher funding costs to compensate equity holders for a smaller balance sheet per dollar of capital. The FY26 Directors' Report explicitly flags navigating 'regulatory changes under the Deposit Takers Act 2023' as an ongoing area of focus.

While the DCS (live from 1 July 2025) appears to be a net positive for deposit-gathering (see Growth Drivers), it is funded over time by levies on all licensed deposit takers including General Finance. As levy rates are phased in, this is a real, if currently modest, ongoing cost that scales with the size of the deposit book — a direct cost of the same scheme that is fuelling GFL's growth.

As an NBDT, General Finance is required to maintain a current credit rating to continue offering products to retail investors. Any future downgrade (e.g. from asset quality deterioration in a rapidly-grown, unseasoned loan book) would likely increase funding costs and could, in a severe scenario, threaten the ability to raise new retail deposits, directly constraining the funding side of the business model.

regulatory.risk: Trust deed and licence covenant compliance
regulatory.description: General Finance's NBDT licence and trust deed impose an 8% minimum capital ratio and other covenants (e.g. the 75% maximum LVR lending policy, the 30% maximum commercial-property lending cap). Breach of any covenant could trigger regulatory intervention, additional reporting, or restrictions on new lending/deposit-taking, directly constraining the growth trajectory the market is currently rewarding.

macro.description: General Finance's collateral base is overwhelmingly NZ residential property (90.3% of security value), concentrated in Auckland. NZ house price forecasts for 2026 are mixed and modest (roughly flat to +5% depending on forecaster, following a period of softness), with the OCR having been cut to 2.25% specifically to support a still-fragile housing and economic recovery. A renewed downturn in Auckland/NZ residential values, higher unemployment, or a slower-than-expected economic recovery would directly increase both default risk on the loan book and downward pressure on recovery values (loan-to-security-value ratios), compounding the risk from the FY26 loan book's rapid, unseasoned growth.

Falling OCR (from a 2023-24 peak) has been a tailwind for loan demand and reduces General Finance's own cost of wholesale/bank deposits, but it also compresses achievable lending yields over time, and a reversal (e.g. RBNZ signalling potential rate increases later in 2026 per some forecasts) would raise borrowing costs for GFL's customers and could increase default risk among highly-levered borrowers.

The FY26 annual report repeatedly describes the operating environment as 'challenging' and 'uncertain,' and explicitly cites the 2026 Iran conflict as a source of economic disruption informing more conservative FY27 growth guidance. As a small NZ-only lender with no revenue diversification outside the domestic economy, General Capital has no offsetting geographic exposure to buffer a domestic downturn.

execution.risk: Sustaining underwriting discipline through a period of rapid scaling
execution.description: Growing the loan book 63% in a single year while maintaining credit quality is operationally demanding — it requires the credit committee, broker network vetting, and valuation processes to scale in lockstep with volume. Past-due loans and impairment metrics actually improved in FY26 (a positive early signal), but the true test of underwriting discipline through this growth phase will only be visible as the FY26 vintage of loans seasons over the next 12-24 months.

The FY26 accounts disclose related-party term deposits (NZ$679,198), related-party loans receivable (NZ$608,167, including a NZ$518,481 capitalised-interest loan and a NZ$112,497 interest-only loan approved during the year), and Key Management Personnel remuneration and expense recharges. While described as arm's-length/normal commercial terms, the overlapping roles of Directors across General Capital and General Finance boards, combined with a small, closely-held shareholder register, warrant ongoing scrutiny of related-party governance.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: The NZ non-bank/NBDT lending sector is a small niche (a handful of rated deposit-taking finance companies) operating alongside a highly concentrated 4-5 bank oligopoly. Demand for non-bank/bridging finance is currently supported by a falling OCR (2.25% as at late 2025) and gradually recovering, though still uncertain, NZ residential property market conditions; NZ house price forecasts for 2026 range from roughly flat to mid-single-digit growth depending on the forecaster. The regulatory backdrop is in a multi-year transition (NBDT Act 2013 to the Deposit Takers Act 2023, full implementation expected around 2028) that will likely raise minimum capital and compliance standards for the sector over time.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High. As a property-secured lender funded by retail deposits, General Capital's credit quality, loan demand and funding costs are all directly tied to the NZ residential property and interest rate cycle. Unlike TAH or ARG-style defensive NZX names, GEN has meaningful earnings and credit-quality sensitivity to a property downturn or a sharp rise in unemployment/interest rates.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate direct sensitivity via net interest margin (a 1% parallel rate shift moves pre-tax profit by ~NZ$342k, ~8.6% of FY26 NPAT, per the FY26 sensitivity disclosure) and higher indirect sensitivity via credit risk (rate rises increase borrower default risk; rate cuts, while supportive of loan demand, compress achievable lending margins over time as competition intensifies).
macro_factors.currency_exposure: None. The Group has no foreign exchange exposure — 100% NZD-denominated assets, liabilities, revenue and costs, entirely within New Zealand.
key_input_costs: Retail term deposit interest rates (GFL's primary funding cost, competing against bank deposit rates and other NBDTs/finance companies for depositor capital)
Credit losses / impairment allowance on the property-secured loan book
Personnel costs (credit, treasury, compliance staff needed to service a rapidly scaling book)
Regulatory/compliance costs (RBNZ supervision, DCS levies, Deposit Takers Act transition costs, credit rating agency fees)

recent_developments.event: General Capital's 2026 Annual Shareholders' Meeting is scheduled for 20 August 2026 in Auckland, including confirmation of auditor Grant Thornton's reappointment, re-election of Managing Director Brent King under NZX rotation rules, and a shareholder vote on a proposed 9.85% increase in the total directors' fee pool to NZ$725,000 per annum.

General Capital released its audited FY26 Annual Report (year ended 31 March 2026): revenue NZ$26.76m (+18%), NPAT NZ$2.72m (-3% YoY, 'broadly in line with prior year'), EPS 2.97 cps (down from 3.09 cps), total assets NZ$283.7m (+30%), total equity NZ$31.3m (+7%), NTA per share 29.31 cps (+11%). General Finance's loan book grew 63%, term deposits grew 34%, and Equifax's outlook on GFL's BB credit rating was upgraded from Stable to Positive (effective 10 December 2025). Directors declared a final dividend of NZ$0.0085/share (plus the NZ$0.0033/share interim), taking FY26 total dividends to NZ$0.0118/share under the new policy (adopted at the July 2025 AGM) of paying up to 40% of NPAT as dividends, with a Dividend Reinvestment Plan offering a 5% discount.

Equifax Australasia reaffirmed General Finance Limited's BB credit rating and upgraded the outlook from 'Stable' to 'Positive', reflecting confidence in the Group's performance and balance sheet growth trajectory.

New Zealand's Depositor Compensation Scheme (DCS) came into effect, providing RBNZ-backed protection of up to NZ$100,000 per eligible depositor per licensed deposit taker (including NBDTs such as General Finance). Management's FY26 disclosures directly attribute a material acceleration in retail term deposit inflows during FY26 to the DCS, which funded the corresponding acceleration in loan book growth.

General Capital's Annual Shareholder Meeting (July 2025) approved a new dividend policy allowing up to 40% of NPAT to be paid out as dividends (replacing/formalising the prior approach), alongside a Dividend Reinvestment Plan with a 5% discount for participants.

General Finance Limited acquired 100% of Bridges Financial Services Limited (insurance premium funding) for total consideration of NZ$7.83m (cash NZ$2.88m plus settlement of a NZ$4.95m original shareholder loan), recognising NZ$1.80m of goodwill; BFSL contributed NZ$507k of revenue and NZ$104k of profit after tax for the five months to 31 March 2025 (FY25 pro-forma full-year contribution estimated at NZ$1.25m of gross revenue).

General Capital executed a 1-for-4 share consolidation, reducing shares on issue and materially restating per-share metrics (NTA/share, NA/share, EPS) for all periods before this date — historical per-share figures pre-August 2024 are not directly comparable without adjustment.

guidance.management_commentary: Directors' Report (FY26): 'The Group achieved a solid result for the year ended 31 March 2026, with revenue up 18% and total assets up 30%, supported by strong growth in term deposits and loan receivables at GFL... The Group remains focused on navigating regulatory changes under the Deposit Takers Act 2023 and sustaining strong financial performance.' On growth funding: 'higher deposit inflows [were] driven by the Deposit Compensation Scheme, which came into effect in July 2025. The demand on the lending side was also strong due to the downward movement of the OCR throughout the year.' On FY27 caution: forecast loan and deposit growth for FY27 is deliberately set below the trailing 3-year average 'to reflect the Group's conservative outlook given economic disruption and uncertainty arising from the 2026 Iran conflict.'

valuation_framing.note: General Capital must be valued as a deposit-taking lender using earnings and book-value-based methods (ROE trend, price-to-book, residual income / excess-return-on-equity), NOT a free-cash-flow DCF. Reported operating cash flow is dominated by loan-book and deposit-book flows that are structural to a growing NBDT balance sheet, not indicative of distributable owner earnings: FY26 net cash used in operating activities was NZ$(24.59)m, driven by NZ$92.0m of net new loan advances only partially offset by NZ$63.2m of net new deposit receipts — a NEGATIVE operating cash flow in a year the company reported healthy NZ$2.72m NPAT. This is entirely normal and expected for a growing bank/NBDT (loan growth is a use of cash, deposit growth is a source of cash, and net new loan growth exceeding net new deposit growth in a single year simply reflects funding some growth from existing liquidity/bank deposits) but would badly mislead a standard FCF-based DCF.
valuation_framing.fy26_roe: Approximately 9.0% (NPAT NZ$2.724m / average total equity of NZ$30.27m, being the simple average of FY25 NZ$29.24m and FY26 NZ$31.30m closing equity) — modest for a lender, reflecting both the still-thin net interest margin (~4.9%) after a ~60-65% cost-to-income ratio, and capital being retained ahead of the growth curve (equity growing only 7% while assets grew 30%).
valuation_framing.fy26_tangible_book_value_per_share: NZ$0.2931 (29.31 cents per share), per the company's own Net Tangible Assets metric (net assets less deferred tax, goodwill and other intangibles, divided by 91,877,912 shares on issue at 31 March 2026), up 11% from NZ$0.2642 at FY25.
valuation_framing.fy26_net_asset_value_per_share: NZ$0.3406 (34.06 cents per share) on a full net-assets (including intangibles) basis.
valuation_framing.implied_price_to_book: At a recent share price in the NZ$0.26-0.30 range (roughly NZ$24-28m market capitalisation on 91.9m shares), GEN trades at approximately 0.76x-0.88x tangible book value and 0.76x-0.88x net asset value — a discount to book that is fairly typical for a sub-investment-grade-rated, illiquid micro-cap NBDT with a ~9% ROE, well below its own Finance-segment pre-tax discount rate of 17.3% used in the FY26 goodwill impairment test (implying management's own cost-of-equity assumption for the core lending business is materially higher than the ~9% ROE currently being earned on it — a useful cross-check that the discount to book is not obviously unwarranted).

bull_case: The Depositor Compensation Scheme (live since 1 July 2025) structurally narrows the safety-perception gap between banks and small rated NBDTs, and management directly credits it with driving the sharp acceleration in FY26 deposit inflows (+34%) that funded 63% loan book growth — if this dynamic persists, General Finance could continue to gather retail deposit funding at a pace disproportionate to its historical scale, a genuine structural tailwind rather than a one-off.

Credit quality metrics actually improved materially in FY26 despite the rapid loan book growth: gross past-due loans fell to 1.8% of the book (from 6.9% in FY25) and Stage 3 credit-impaired balances fell to nil (from NZ$2.76m) — an early positive signal that underwriting discipline has, so far, kept pace with volume growth, and the credit rating outlook was upgraded to Positive on the back of it.

A falling OCR is simultaneously supporting borrower loan demand and (over time) should reduce GFL's marginal cost of retail deposit funding, a favourable combination for NIM and volume growth as long as the rate-cutting cycle continues and doesn't reverse sharply.

Trading at roughly 0.76x-0.88x tangible book value against a growing balance sheet and a management team with a long tenure (Managing Director since 2018, previously 17 years running the Dorchester Group) and meaningful personal share ownership (Brent King/Snowdon Peak ~10.45%) offers an asymmetric setup if the loan book continues to scale profitably and ROE improves from its current sub-10% level toward the ~17% pre-tax discount rate management itself uses to value the Finance segment.

The 40%-of-NPAT dividend policy (adopted July 2025) with a 5% DRP discount provides a modest but real cash yield while still retaining the majority of earnings to fund continued balance sheet growth, giving shareholders participation in both income and compounding book value per share (NTA/share +11% in FY26 alone).
bear_case: A 62.7% one-year expansion of a property-secured loan book, funded by a similarly rapid but shorter-tenor deposit base, is a textbook precursor to future credit and liquidity stress — the FY26 book is largely unseasoned, and the true test of underwriting quality through this growth phase will not be visible until the FY26 vintage matures over the next 12-24 months, by which point any deterioration would already be baked into a much larger balance sheet.

General Capital is a sub-investment-grade-rated (Equifax BB), thinly-capitalised (7% equity growth against 30% asset growth in FY26), NZD-only, single-city-concentrated (76% of loans in Auckland) micro-cap lender with structurally weak return on equity (~9% FY26) relative to its own management's 17.3% cost-of-equity assumption for the core Finance business — the current price-to-book discount may be entirely rational rather than a mispricing opportunity.

The multi-year transition from the NBDT Act 2013 to the Deposit Takers Act 2023 (full implementation expected around 2028, with capital-standard and risk-weight consultations ongoing through 2026) is a real and largely uncontrollable regulatory overhang for a company this small; materially higher minimum capital requirements designed with larger institutions in mind could force a dilutive capital raise, slower growth, or higher funding costs.

Extreme shareholder concentration (top holder 34.5%, top 5 holders 66.4%, top 20 holders 88.6% of shares on issue) and micro-cap illiquidity mean the stock is difficult to enter or exit in size, is exposed to governance/related-party risk given the closely-held register and overlapping director roles across General Capital and General Finance, and offers minimal institutional scrutiny or analyst coverage to independently validate management's credit and growth assumptions.

The company remains entirely exposed to a single, cyclical, correlated risk factor — the NZ (and specifically Auckland) residential property market — with no offsetting geographic or asset-class diversification; a renewed property downturn, a reversal of the OCR-cutting cycle, or a deposit-market liquidity event (company-specific or sector-wide) would hit credit quality, funding costs and loan demand simultaneously.
